extracted.intended_audience: researchers and policymakers studying peer review and gender bias; journal editors, publishers, and scientometrics scholars
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing gender bias in peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Statistical and network analysis of whether peer review and editorial processes penalize or favor manuscripts by women across 145 scholarly journals; includes modeling editorial referee selection, referee recommendations, and editorial decisions while controlling for covariates. Uses mixed-effects Bayesian models, Poisson regression, and a Bayesian-learning network.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial selection of referees
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial selection of referees (step i) — actions performed by editors in inviting and selecting referees to review manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured whether manuscripts with a higher proportion of women among authors were more usually reviewed by women referees; controlled for number of authors, journal impact factor, and peer review model (single vs double blind). Considered as a possible source of bias linked to gender matching between authors and referees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee recommendations (review score)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referee recommendations aggregated into a review score (step ii) used to represent reviewers' evaluations of manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referee recommendations were recoded into an ordinal scale (reject, major revisions, minor revisions, accept). A review score per manuscript was computed using counts of potential recommendation combinations (#worse, #better) via reviewScore = #worse/(#better + #worse). Treated as a proxy for manuscript quality and included as a predictor and mediator in models; reported field-specific effects (e.g., women received more positive reviews in biomedicine and social sciences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Final editorial decision (accept/reject)
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial decision on the manuscript (step iii) — whether the manuscript was accepted (final decision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeled with logistic mixed-effects models (random effects for journals) and with the Bayesian network. Models included review scores and other controls; models explained over 80% of the outcome variance when including review scores. Sensitivity and specificity of predictions were reported (e.g., ~0.93 sensitivity, ~0.96 specificity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion of women among authors (AutRatFem)
rubrics_metrics.description: AutRatFem — the ratio/proportion of women authors on a manuscript, used as a main predictor of referee recommendations and editorial decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in primary models and alternative specifications; evidence reported by field (positive effect in biomedicine and physical sciences in some analyses). Alternative gender specifications (first/last author, five author groups) were also tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion of women among referees (RevRatFem)
rubrics_metrics.description: RevRatFem — the ratio/proportion of women among the referees assigned to a manuscript, used as a predictor and mediator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Found that manuscripts with higher proportion of women authors tended to be reviewed by more women referees; the proportion of women referees had field-specific associations with acceptance and rounds of revision (sometimes negative effect on acceptance; sometimes associated with more revision rounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: First author gender
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender of the first author (FirstAuthorGender) used as a predictor in alternative model specifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeled effects by field; e.g., manuscripts with a woman first author were more favorably treated in physical sciences and less in life sciences (field-dependent, often weak effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Last author gender
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender of the last author (LastAuthorGender) used as a predictor in alternative model specifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally found no systematic effect on acceptance except a weak negative effect in biomedical and health sciences in some specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author composition groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Five mutually exclusive groups of authors: man sole author, woman sole author, all-men teams, all-women teams, and co-ed teams of authors — used as predictors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to check robustness of gender effects; overall no systematic bias against manuscripts submitted by women when considering these groups, though complex interactions with field were observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review type (single- vs double-blind)
rubrics_metrics.description: PRType — type of peer review adopted by the journal (single-blind versus double-blind) included as a covariate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included in models as a control; single-blind status sometimes associated with higher acceptance probability in certain fields. Also examined interactions (e.g., manuscripts by women received worse reviews in social science journals using single-blind review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal impact factor (IFRounded)
rubrics_metrics.description: IFRounded — the journal's impact factor (rounded) used as a control variable to ensure comparability across journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included in mixed-effects and logistic models; reported coefficient signs and credible intervals by field. Journals were limited to those in the Journal Citation Report and with an impact factor for comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of authors (nAuthors)
rubrics_metrics.description: nAuthors — the number of coauthors on the manuscript, included as a covariate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controlled for because team size may affect reviewer selection, review scores, and acceptance. Coefficients reported per-field in models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of referees (nRev)
rubrics_metrics.description: nRev — the number of referees assigned to a manuscript, included as a covariate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Found negative association between number of referees and acceptance probability in models; also positively associated with number of revision rounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of revision rounds (NumRounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: NumRounds — the number of review/revision rounds a manuscript underwent before acceptance; analyzed via Poisson regression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poisson regression predicted NumRounds; generally no robust effect of author gender on number of rounds. More women among reviewer teams often associated with higher probability of more rounds (except social sciences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee agreement score (Agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreement — a score measuring agreement between referee recommendations for a manuscript (one minus proportion of recommendations to change to reach perfect agreement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculated to allow comparability across manuscripts with different numbers of referees; included as covariate in models (positive association with acceptance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of referee recommendations as proxy for manuscript quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Because an objective measure of manuscript quality was unavailable, referee recommendations were used as a control/proxy for manuscript quality in analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note limitations: referee recommendations imperfectly measure intrinsic quality; models used recommendations to detect editorial bias after accounting for quality signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review score calculation method
rubrics_metrics.description: Method to compute reviewScore per manuscript: recode each referee recommendation into ordinal categories, derive all possible unique combinations (potential recommendation set), count #worse and #better, then compute reviewScore = #worse/(#better + #worse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reviewScore is independent of the number of referees and was scaled (multiplied by 100 in tables) for interpretability. Agreement score computed as complement of necessary changes to reach perfect agreement divided by number of referees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed-effects Bayesian modeling with random journal effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of linear and logistic mixed-effect models estimated in a Bayesian framework with random effects for journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models estimated using brms (R), four independent chains with 10,000 iterations (5,000 burn-in + 5,000 sampling), flat priors (zero mean), convergence verified with scale reduction factors R-hat < 1.01; Bayes factors reported for β > 0, pseudo-R2 computed per recommended approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bayesian-learning network to model complex interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: A Bayesian network (Bayesian-learning network) was estimated to capture complex interactions and indirect paths of bias across variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trained on 80% of manuscripts and tested on 20% for validation; structure learned through multiple constraint- and score-based algorithms and aggregated by including links found by ≥70% of algorithms; restrictions forbade links from review score and editorial decision to other nodes and chronologically impossible links. Used to compute conditional probabilities and overall prediction accuracy (~82%). Directionality of arrows interpreted cautiously (not strict causation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-specific modeling / separated models by scientific field
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate models estimated for each field of research (biomedicine and health, life sciences, physical sciences, social sciences and humanities) to account for field-specific effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowed capturing different effects of author/referee gender and interactions in each field; Bayesian network retained scientific field as linked to all nodes (not shown for readability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling imbalanced data
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition and handling of imbalance (e.g., fewer women authors/referees, overrepresentation of physical sciences) in dataset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostics were used to confirm imbalances did not affect results (tables S6); authors decided not to rebalance data manually to avoid loss of information given many variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender inference (gender guessing) procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Three-step gender inference procedure: (1) use salutations if available; (2) query gender-guesser with first names and country; (3) query Gender API and use returned gender when minimum sample and accuracy thresholds met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritized accuracy; did not accept gender-guesser outputs categorized mostly_man/mostly_woman/andy/unknown; used Gender API only when at least 62 samples with ≥57% accuracy; aimed to keep misclassification below ~5% per benchmarks. Resulted in estimated gender for ~77% of authors and ~82% of referees; remaining assigned unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data inclusion criteria for journals and manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals included were those in the Journal Citation Report (Web of Science) with an impact factor; dataset originally had 157 journals but analyses focused on 145 journals and 348,223 submissions (manuscripts sent out to referees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To ensure comparability, only journals with WoS impact factor considered; because desk rejection data were not consistently available, analyses concentrated on manuscripts that were sent out for review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model diagnostics, priors, and inference reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for model estimation and reporting: use of flat priors, multiple chains, iteration counts, R-hat checks, reporting of mean estimates, 95% credible intervals, and Bayes factors (for β > 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used recommended statistical practices (brms, Stan) and reporting conventions; pseudo-R2 computed using recommended approach; interpretation of Bayes factors followed standard recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prediction performance reporting (sensitivity/specificity, accuracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report prediction performance metrics for models: sensitivity, specificity, and overall accuracy (e.g., Bayesian network predicted acceptance with 82% accuracy; logistic models sensitivity ~0.92–0.93 and specificity ~0.95–0.97).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these metrics to assess model fit and predictive validity; inform interpretation of effect sizes and robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls and confounders to include
rubrics_metrics.description: Include controls for proportion of women among referees, journal impact factor, number of coauthors, type of peer review, review scores, number of referees, agreement, and number of revision rounds when modeling gender effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly control for these covariates to isolate gender effects and avoid confounding; models tested different specifications and alternative gender variables (first/last author, author groups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and caveats to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledged limitations such as lack of objective manuscript quality measure, inability to estimate pool of potential authors/referees, possible influence of author seniority/institutional prestige/ethnicity, and data-sharing limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly report these limitations and avoid overinterpreting directionality of Bayesian network paths as causation; recommend further data integration and randomized experiments where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data sharing and reproducibility practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Make dataset available (link provided) and comply with data sharing protocol (PEERE Protocol for Data Sharing); provide supplementary materials and code details for reproducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide access to underlying records required to rerun analyses while preserving journal anonymity per protocol; encourage publishers and independent groups to share peer-review data to facilitate research.
